_comment: Throughput baseline for bench/regression-gate.sh. Raising this is a
deliberate act in a commit, the same as the documentation ratchets in
tests/docs_drift_test.rs. Do NOT lower it to make a red run pass: that
records a regression as the new normal, which is precisely how the 0.5.84
drop survived four releases.
The figure is 4-core offline reconstruction over the fixed-state 535k
corpus that bench/carrier.py generates (5000 calls, 100 Call-IDs, 200
streams). Four cores is now both the peak of the curve and its most
reproducible point -- 2.28 / 2.28 / 2.35M across three replicates here.
It was chosen when it was NOT the peak, and the reason it gives has since
inverted: the 2-core peak of the time spanned ~2% run to run, so four was
picked for reproducibility instead. 0.5.89 moved the frame-provenance
digest off the sequential reader onto the workers and the peak moved to
four. The measurement point did not have to change -- only the
justification for it. Said plainly because the old wording ("four cores
rather than the 2-core peak") now contradicts docs/benchmarks.md.
Measured on a LOCAL release build of the recorded commit, not on a release
artifact -- the gate has to catch a regression the day it lands, not once
it has shipped. The two are close but NOT identical here: this local build
medianed 2.28M while the published 0.5.91 artifact measured 2.32M over the
same corpus, a ~1.7% gap sitting inside run-to-run spread. The baseline
follows the local build, because a local build is what CI rebuilds and
compares. The earlier claim that the two 'agree' was true of 0.5.89 and is
now only approximately true, so it is stated as a measured gap rather than
as agreement.

measured.host: NVIDIA Jetson Thor devboard (aarch64), 14 cores, PREEMPT_RT, idle
measured.method: median-of-5 after one discarded warmup, three replicates
measured.idle_gate: vmstat id >= 96% and no toolchain build process; 90% would permit 1.4 busy cores on a 14-core host

_floor_rationale: The regression this gate exists to catch was 40%. Run-to-run spread is ~2%
on an idle host and ~10% when something else shares it, so 20% sits clear
of both. A tighter band on a runner that also serves CI would be flaky in
the direction that gets a gate muted, and a muted gate catches nothing.
Sanity check against real numbers, recomputed against this baseline rather
than carried over: 0.5.88 measured 1.33M here, which is 58% and trips the
floor. 0.5.83 measured 2.02M, which is 89% and does not. The floor itself
Note what the raise fixed. While this file still baselined 0.5.89's 1.89M,
the floor sat at 1.51M against a tool running at 2.28M -- a 34% drop would
have passed a gate whose stated band is 20%. A stale baseline does not
merely under-report; it silently widens the band it advertises.
